newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland struggles to shake off the sterling blues.
newsitem.headline: Ireland struggles to shake off the sterling blues.

text.p: Ireland's central bank should be celebrating. It can boast booming growth, low inflation, and one of the few European Union economies which currently qualifies for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

But the unruly antics of its neighbour's currency are spoiling the party. Whenever Ireland appears to be waltzing smoothly towards EMU, sterling appears like a malign spectre to disrupt the celebrations.

Currency market gyrations are threatening Ireland's chances of entering a single currency, economists say. And some argue that the country's current predicament shows that entering EMU without Britain, Ireland's largest single trading partner, could lead to disaster.

"It highlights an inconsistency in terms of Ireland taking part in EMU," said Oliver Mangan, senior economist at Davy Stockbrokers. "There are dangers for us from our relationship with sterling, which don't exist for other EU countries."
A few months ago the problem for Ireland was that the British currency was too weak. Now it's sterling's strength that is giving the Irish central bank a headache.

But the underlying problem remains the same. Ireland's close economic ties with Britain make the punt/sterling exchange rate crucial for the Irish economy. But Ireland's EMU aspirations require it to pursue exchange-rate stability against the mark.
So the Irish central bank has to try to track both sterling and the mark. And when the British and German currencies are heading in different directions, things begin to get tricky.
When the punt is strong versus sterling, as in August when it cleared 1.04 stg, exporters to the UK complain they are being squeezed out of business and the threat of job losses looms.

When the punt is weak -- it fell below parity with sterling last week for the first time in 18 months -- economists warn that import price rises could stoke up inflation in an economy growing at the fastest rate in the EU.
But if the central bank tries to track sterling to avoid these dangers, it can stumble into other pitfalls.

Sterling is outside the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) and may not joing a single currency in the first wave, so it is often out of step with the mark. If the Irish pound follows sterling it risks dangerous volatility within the ERM.

Sterling's current strength has pulled the Irish pound above 2.50 marks, its highest levels in more than three years and above the upper limit of the old 2.25 percent ERM bands which were in force until the currency turbulence of mid-1993.
According to some interpretations of the Maastricht criteria for EMU entry, currencies may have to have stayed within these notional bands for at least two years prior to EMU to qualify.

So the central bank faces a dilemma. If it follows sterling, its resultant volatility may disqualify it for EMU. But if it tracks the mark, it risks an inflationary boom which will also scupper its single-currency hopes.

Some economists say Ireland's problems with sterling should be seen as a clear warning that entering EMU could lead to severe problems if Britain stays out. "Since the introduction of the wide ERM bands, the Irish pound has been by far the most volatile currency in the ERM because of our relationship with sterling," Mangan said.

"If we go into EMU there will still be a lot of trade going on with the UK but we lose that exchange rate flexibilty," he said. "Sterling will affect Irish inflation and therefore effective interest rates, and a volatile sterling would create all the ingrediants for a boom and bust cycle in Ireland."

Others, however, say Ireland could learn to survive in monetary union even without Britain. "The central bank's options are not great, but if sterling is outside monetary union and is volatile we have got to learn to live with it," said Jim Power, chief economist at Bank of Ireland Group Treasury.
He said wage flexibility and a balanced budget could help mitigate the problem. "That would give us a lot more scope to deal with sterling down the road."
